новый карандаш is masculine singular nominative; новая машина is feminine singular nominative. The adjective agrees with the noun in the phrase, so the car phrase uses the feminine form но́вая rather than masculine но́вый or plural но́вые. To make a feminine singular noun phrase accusative, change both words: the adjective но́вая becomes но́вую, and the noun кни́га becomes кни́гу. Both words change in these supplied case pairs.

The dictionary form of this adjective is masculine singular nominative но́вый. A phrase can need another gender, number or case even though the dictionary form is masculine singular nominative. In the neuter, the adjective но́вое becomes но́вого in the genitive, and the noun окно́ becomes окна́. Both adjective and noun change case while remaining neuter singular.

новое платье is neuter singular nominative. Compare the adjective with the masculine pencil and feminine car examples above: the noun controls the agreement required in that phrase. синий стол uses the masculine nominative form of a different adjective meaning dark blue. Learn the forms of each adjective as you meet them.

синяя книга and синее письмо show feminine and neuter singular nominative agreement for the adjective meaning dark blue. Keep the noun and the requested agreement in view. Use these nominative examples as models, then check the case the task names.

синие книги has plural nominative agreement. For the adjective meaning new, но́вый is masculine singular nominative and но́вые is plural nominative. For the plural nominative of the same adjective as но́вый, choose но́вые rather than feminine singular но́вая. The comparison changes number; it does not change the adjective to a different vocabulary item.

но́вая and но́вое are feminine and neuter singular nominative forms of the same adjective. The corresponding dictionary form is masculine singular nominative но́вый. When the task shows но́вая and asks for that dictionary form, choose но́вый rather than neuter но́вое. Use the requested gender, number and case to decide the answer.

но́вые is plural nominative of this adjective. Compare all four nominative forms: но́вый, но́вая, но́вое and но́вые. A feminine singular phrase such as новая машина needs но́вая, not the masculine dictionary form or the plural form.

These basic counting examples use nominative phrases. The related noun-case pattern also applies in inanimate accusative contexts, with the appropriate noun form. Other sentence cases require numeral declension as well as noun declension. A count ending in one outside the teen exception uses a nominative singular noun in the shown basic phrases. один час — один час. два часа — два часа. 

A count ending in two, three or four outside the teen exception uses a genitive singular noun in the basic construction. This is a grammatical singular form even though the count is greater than one.

Counts ending in zero or five through nine use genitive plural in the basic construction. The teen exception also uses genitive plural. Ten and sixteen therefore fit this pattern. пять часов — пять часов. двадцать один час — двадцать один час. 

For a compound count, inspect the last two digits first. If they are 11, 12, 13 or 14, use genitive plural for the counted noun in the basic construction. Otherwise, the final digit selects the pattern: one, two-through-four, or zero/five-through-nine. Compare 21 and 22: their final digits select different noun cases; being larger than five is not enough to choose genitive plural. двадцать два часа — двадцать два часа. две девушки — two girls.

For 15 through19 the final digit already leads to genitive plural;11 through14 override the one/two/three/four ending pattern. пять девушек — five girls. шестнадцать рублей — sixteen rubles. 

The example with 41 follows the final-one pattern and uses nominative singular for the counted noun. The example with 10 follows the zero-ending pattern and uses genitive plural. десять копеек — ten kopeks. сорок один год — forty-one years.

In the simple possession pattern shown here, the possessor after the possession preposition is genitive. The thing possessed is nominative. The schematic slot in the first example represents that possessed thing. У меня есть Х — I have X. У вас есть сын? — Do you have a son? 

A simple positive possession line places the possessed thing in the nominative. An absence line places the absent thing in the genitive. Decide whether the whole shown line affirms or denies possession.

The son examples keep the same simple possession pattern in a statement or question: genitive possessor and nominative possessed thing. The form of a question does not turn the noun into an absence construction. Да, у меня есть сын. — Yes, I have a son. У твоего́ му́жа есть оди́н друг — Your husband has one friend. 

The many-friends example includes a quantity expression. Quantity patterns are separate from the simple nominative possessed thing in the son checks. The no-son example below denies possession and uses the genitive for the absent thing. У моего нового мужа есть много друзе́й — My new husband has many friends. У меня́ нет сы́на — No, I don't have a son. 

The no-money example also denies possession. Choose the genitive absence explanation, rather than the simple positive possession explanation. У моего́ бра́та нет де́нег — My brother doesn't have any money.

идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они у́летят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

Мы идём в библиотеку. — We are headed to the library. Птицы летят на юг. — The birds are flying south. These supplied contexts show Motion in progress in one direction (imperfective). Ребёнок ходит шесть месяцев. — The child has been walking for six months. This is General walking ability (imperfective). Мы ходили по городу весь день. — We walked around the city all day. This is Movement in various directions (imperfective). Directionality is a property of the whole supplied use, not an English lexical gloss or an automatic claim that the traveller arrived. The basic unprefixed pairs are imperfective.

Она ходит в супермаркет каждую неделю. — She goes to the supermarket every week. This is Repeated trips (imperfective). В прошлом году я ездил в Россию. — I went to Russia (and returned) last year. In the retained supplied context this is One completed round trip in the past (imperfective). The past round-trip interpretation includes a return; the unprefixed form nevertheless remains imperfective. A choice saying “The form is perfective because this trip is completed.” makes an incorrect aspect inference for these forms. Do not equate a destination with unidirectionality or event completion with perfective aspect. Prefixed setting-out and path examples require their separately taught meanings.
